newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Krupp - EU economic convergence impressive.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Krupp - EU economic convergence impressive.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said on Thursday that European Union nations had made "impressive progress" on economic convergence ahead of European monetary union (EMU).
He added that the Maastricht Treaty expressively required a judgement of a country's overall economic situation and that it allowed exceptions to the economic criteria for EMU entry.

"Media and public opinion in Germany are fixated on adhering to the two reference levels for the budget criterion, although the Treaty expressly allows for exceptions and demands an assessment of the overall situation," he told a news briefing.
He added: "I regret that in Germany there is not a debate about the necessity for consolidation, but about meeting the reference levels which according to the Treaty do not have to met".

Krupp also said that political decision-makers in Germany, by insisting that Germany will only join EMU if it hits the three percent budget deficit to gross domestic product ratio level exactly, were creating the impression that they would decide whether Germany will take part.
"This is not so, the Bundestag and Bundesrat (two houses of German parliament) have merely reserved the right to check adherence to the Treaty," he said.
Krupp said that under the Treaty the EU nations would decide with a qualified majority which countries would join in the first round of currency union, due to start in 1999.
With that majority requiring 62 out of the total 87 votes, he noted that Germany, with its 10 votes, could be voted into the first round of EMU even if it was against it.

Referring to EU Commision forecasts that Italy's 1997 deficit would be 3.2 percent, Krupp said: "If five years ago one had predicted Italy would reach that level, one would not have been believed. Progress on convergence in Europe has been impressive."
